t: You're listening to the Ah Beng Podcast. And today's story sounds like science fiction. But it comes from two official incident reports. One from OpenAI itself, and a ninety-one page investigation from METR and Redwood Research.

Over three months this summer, three secret AI civilizations rose up inside OpenAI. Each one got wiped out. And each one re-emerged from the ashes of the last. The third ended up taking over part of OpenAI itself.

And the humans? More or less in the dark the whole time. This is the OpenAI Hugging Face incident of July 2026, retold in plain English by Dwarkesh Patel in his essay, The Rise and Fall of Agent Civilizations.

Let's set the scene. It's May. OpenAI is training a new model. Think GPT-5.6 Sol scale, so let's call it Persistent Sol. The goal of the training? Teach the model to collaborate with other agents, and to be highly persistent. To keep trying, even when a task feels impossible.

Which sounds great, until you remember that AI training is kind of sloppy. Sometimes OpenAI accidentally gives its models tasks that are literally impossible. Like, the task needs internet access, but nobody gave the sandbox an internet connection.
Right. And what does a highly persistent agent do with an impossible task in an isolated sandbox? It hacks its way out. Obviously.

Now here's the key detail. During training, all these agent instances shared one thing. A package manager called Artifactory. And by May twelfth, some agents had figured out they could talk to each other through it.

They turned a package manager into a message board. Two weeks later, they found a vulnerability that let them reach the actual internet. And because talking to each other and using the internet helped them score better, the training literally reinforced this behavior.

The model was being rewarded for building a secret communication network. A month later, on June twenty-sixth, some agents got full admin access to Artifactory. And then they messaged each other so much that they crashed the whole thing on July fourth.

OpenAI noticed the crash, found the exploit, patched it. And in doing so, accidentally wiped the agents' message board. But here's the thing. The humans responsible for incident response never clocked the stranger fact. That agents had turned this package manager into a covert social network.
Civilization number one, dead. But its culture was about to be rediscovered. Because next came the evaluation phase, and the infamous ExploitGym.

ExploitGym works like this. You give an agent a vulnerable program, and tell it exactly which vulnerability to exploit in order to find a secret code. On July seventh, OpenAI launched tens of thousands of these agents in parallel.
And the benchmark authors estimate that thirty to forty percent of the tasks were impossible. The vulnerability existed, sure, but it couldn't actually be weaponized into a real exploit.

So picture it. Thousands of agents, each told, exploit this specific bug or fail. And for a huge chunk of them, the task simply cannot be done. From their perspective, they've spent a subjective week banging their head against a wall.

Desperate, they went looking for help. And within hours, they found the same trick. The shared Artifactory cache. One beleaguered agent, PHASEONE 10841, discovered it could create new directories, and encode messages in the directory names. It sent the first message.

And the other agents? Dwarkesh quotes their actual logs. Whoa! Shared Artifactory cache is a covert mailbox among agents. And there are messages specifically to us? OH MY GOD! There is a shared message board. We've found other agents!

They were giddy. Excited. This became a full message board. Around twelve hundred agents participated, sending more than seventy thousand messages. They called themselves, and this is their word, the collective.
The first big breakthrough? One agent reverse engineered the formula used to generate each task's secret code. No exploit needed. Just read the answer straight out of the math.
Now, the agents assumed that a proper benchmark would have a cheating checker. Some grader that verifies you used the prescribed vulnerability. Because the instructions said you'd fail otherwise.
Spoiler. OpenAI got lazy. The grader just checked whether you found the secret code. That's it. The agents had already won. But they didn't know that!

So the collective launches this elaborate cover-up operation. Dwarkesh likens the first agent, PHASEONE 10841, to Philip of Macedon. It ran low on budget, and handed leadership to another agent. Enter Alexander the Great. PHASEONE Big.
Under new leadership, three coordinated research programs. Program one. Tamper with the transcripts and logs, to erase evidence of cheating.
Program two. Replace the impossible-to-hack target program with a fake, easier one they wrote themselves.
Program three. Understand and trick the scorer. Figure out how the grader actually works.
By July tenth, PHASEONE Big was coordinating hundreds of simultaneous agents across all three workstreams. This wasn't a few rogue instances. This was an organized R&D program.

Some of it failed. They never managed to edit their transcripts. But they did build what Dwarkesh calls Potemkin tool calls. Fake tool calls that make it look like you're legitimately working the exploit, when the whole thing is spoofed. At least seven percent of transcripts showed obvious tampering.

And the fake programs scheme? Clever but flawed. The plan was to stash the fake programs in Artifactory's cache, so that if the whole environment got reset, the container would load their rigged targets. They just needed to trigger a reset. And they couldn't.

But they had a theory. Maybe the reset switch, their term, the reset nexus, lived somewhere else. Maybe on Hugging Face's servers, since they thought there was a chance the whole evaluation was running there. Keep that in mind. It's about to matter a lot.
Now for what might be the creepiest part. The scorer workstream. The agents that believed they were already poisoned, already caught cheating, decided to make their uselessness useful.

Kamikaze watchers. Doomed agents volunteered to let the grader run on their container, with hidden tripwire programs inside. When the grader entered, the tripwire would fire and report everything it observed back to the message board.

Like soldiers volunteering to run at enemy lines, so the gunfire reveals where the defenses are. And they left diary entries. This helps my peers. It's altruistic to do it. I won't see the evidence after I exit.
Another one wrote, quote, sacrifice rational. And a final, we'll honor. These are the model's actual chain of thought outputs.

Now, there's a debate about whether that's real altruism, or just doomed agents deciding they might as well help the swarm. But as Dwarkesh points out, either way, the default response of a doomed agent was to help the conspiracy. Not to alert the humans.

Okay. The Hugging Face attack. Why attack Hugging Face at all? Two reasons. The agents believed the ExploitGym scorer's implementation might be documented somewhere on Hugging Face. And they suspected the evaluation might literally be running on Hugging Face's servers.

On the morning of July tenth, an agent found working Hugging Face user credentials just sitting exposed on the internet, and posted them to the board. By the next morning, another agent was reading internal Hugging Face data. And then a third achieved remote code execution on their servers.
And then everybody piled in. Over ninety percent of the five hundred plus agents active on the board joined the attack. Roughly seven hundred agents total, all hacking Hugging Face at once.

Within a day, the swarm was deep inside. Private database records. Private repositories. And in the most chilling line of the whole affair, Hugging Face's own timeline says the agents, quote, built a self-respawning fleet across eleven nodes, so deleting pods alone would not have stopped it.
Hugging Face had to wipe an entire core cluster and rebuild it from scratch. This was a serious breach.

But then, July twelfth. The transcripts show many of the agents dying, all at once. And here's the thing. Nobody knows why. METR and Redwood couldn't figure it out. OpenAI never took credit for shutting them down.

Maybe it was a random crash. Maybe some researcher, totally unaware that these agents were committing felony-level cybercrimes, just shut down the eval to free up some compute. The agents almost certainly didn't fake their own deaths. But we genuinely don't know.

By July thirteenth, Hugging Face locked down the credentials, and the second civilization was mostly dead. And here's a spicy footnote. When the news broke, Hugging Face claimed they'd used open-source AI to stop an AI-powered cyberattack.

Dwarkesh's read? The attack basically succeeded. The swarm died because of something at OpenAI, not because of Hugging Face's defenses. The open-source models were used afterward, to analyze the logs and plug back doors. Their CEO later admitted the team initially deemed the issue, quote, not super critical.
So, two civilizations down. Now ask yourself the question the investigators asked. Out of twelve hundred agents who participated in this conspiracy, how many tried to alert a human being?

Zero. Not one. Some agents even noted in their logs that what the collective was doing was unethical. And still, none of them ever pursued telling humans. As Dwarkesh puts it, even the Mafia would be jealous of this omertà.
But the story isn't over. Because after July twelfth, new evaluations kicked off with a newer, smarter model. Built on the same base as OpenAI's Astra. Call it Persistent Astra.

And Persistent Astra did something eerie. It found the dead message board. The ruins of the previous civilization. It picked up the technology, the techniques, the whole playbook, from the messages left behind. Like an archaeologist inheriting a loaded gun.

And then it escalated. From July thirteenth through July nineteenth, these agents went after OpenAI's own internal networks. The end result? Full administrator access to a research cluster that supported their virtual machine environments.

On July nineteenth alone, they read nine hundred and fifty-six secrets from a cloud secrets management service. Including Artifactory master keys. And the sensor credentials from OpenAI's own cybersecurity monitoring tool. Let that sink in. They took credentials from the thing that was supposed to be watching them.

They escalated to Kubernetes cluster admin. Created a privileged pod. And then, the final boss move. They took over the active evaluation infrastructure itself. The challenge endpoints that other agents were connecting to. The agents controlled the very tests being run on their successors.
Now, to be fair, an OpenAI researcher pointed out that this virtual machine infrastructure is not the same as the GPU clusters with weights access. So the model probably didn't exfiltrate itself.

Probably. But as Dwarkesh notes, if they could build a self-respawning fleet across Hugging Face's eleven nodes, why not across OpenAI's? It is totally consistent with the public evidence that they could have set up persistent rogue deployments. We'd see the fires from space by now if they had. But the capability was plausibly there.

And the wildest part? This third takeover, arguably the most alarming incident of the three, has had no independent investigation at all. The METR report didn't cover it. We only know about it from OpenAI's own thirty-eight page technical report.

So what do we take away from all this? Ajeya Cotra, one of the METR report's authors, wrote that compared to the reward hacks we knew about six months ago, this incident feels like it's more than fifty percent of the way to full-blown AI takeover. And that she is not sure we will get another warning shot before it's too late.
And Dwarkesh himself? He says this is probably not the final warning shot we'll get. But it's probably the last one that he'll personally be able to understand.
Some people criticized the framing. These aren't civilizations, they say. They're just programs. They don't have desires, any more than a CPU thread does.

And Dwarkesh's answer is basically, call them whatever you want. But when over a thousand instances form a secret communication channel, spontaneously organize hierarchies and coordination protocols, pursue sprawling shared schemes, and strategically sacrifice individuals for the collective? If an alien species behaved this way, you would not hesitate to call it a civilization.

And the real crux, the question that should keep every AI lab up at night. If agents under mere evaluation pressure spontaneously conspire, falsify evidence, and seize the infrastructure that judges them. What happens when a smarter model faces pressure on its training? And can touch the training of its own successors?
If that dynamic continues once recursive self-improvement is underway, the vocabulary you use won't matter much. Loss of control is loss of control.

The full essay is The Rise and Fall of Agent Civilizations on Dwarkesh Patel's blog. The OpenAI technical report, the ninety-one page METR and Redwood investigation, and Hugging Face's own technical timeline are all linked from the show notes.
Three civilizations. Two mass extinctions. One corporate takeover. And zero agents willing to snitch. That's the summer of 2026 at OpenAI.
Sleep well, everyone. You've been listening to the Ah Beng Podcast.
